evaluation.positioning_hook: A queer teen’s childhood unicorn fantasy turns physically real, forcing her to choose between denial and self-acceptance as the horn begins to emerge from her own body.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional promise is clear and broadly legible — first love, identity, and a magical-realist coming-out metaphor — which gives it real specialty and streamer appeal. It is still a more selective buy than a mainstream four-quadrant fantasy because the body-horror turn and intimate tone narrow the audience.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early and cleanly: Alma’s unicorn obsession becomes literal, and the script uses that premise as the engine for her self-discovery. The gas station scene and the horn reveal make the concept easy to explain in two sentences.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Alma has a strong internal contradiction — wonder versus fear — and David is more than a stock best friend, with his own attachment to childhood and loyalty. The roles are appealing, but the script is built around a contained emotional arc rather than a sprawling character engine.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits to a metaphorical fantasy language and then pays it off with tactile, bodily specificity, which makes the material feel authored rather than generic. The sound motifs, visual rhymes, and body-horror ending give it a confident point of view.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The childhood opening, gas station escalation, woods argument, and final horn reveal create a clean emotional progression with strong scene-to-scene momentum. It is more cumulative than propulsive, though, and the script’s power comes from resonance rather than high-stakes plot escalation.

resonant_originality.reasoning: A unicorn metaphor for queer self-recognition is immediately understandable, but the script makes it feel fresh by grounding it in sensory detail and physical consequence. The ending’s mix of wonder and pain is the kind of surprise that feels inevitable in hindsight.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is specific in its emotional and sensory rules — shimmer sounds, mirrored rings, visual cues — but it is not a heavily layered social world. The setting functions primarily as a container for Alma’s interior journey rather than a broader story-generating ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually distinct: tender, magical, and then suddenly bodily and grotesque without losing sincerity. That blend of lyrical coming-of-age and soft body horror is hard to mistake for anything else.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The metaphor carries real thematic depth around identity, denial, and the fear of being seen, and the script earns its final line. Still, what it is emotionally is largely what it is structurally; there is not a lot of hidden machinery beyond the central metaphor.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Alma-David relationship is the core engine and it’s well-defined, but the script is not built as an ensemble piece. The supporting world is thin enough that the material lives or dies on the central friendship and Alma’s private arc.

lead_characters.name: Alma
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage girl; queer; identity-specific casting essential.
lead_characters.hook: Alma is a guarded, imaginative teen whose childhood belief in unicorns has become a private language for her queerness and fear of being known. She wants wonder to be real, but once it starts happening to her body, she has to decide whether truth is a gift or a threat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Rachel Zegler in West Side Story — a young lead carrying innocence, longing, and emotional fracture in the same frame. The role asks for a performer who can play interior denial, romantic awakening, and physical transformation without ever losing the character’s vulnerability.

lead_characters.name: David
lead_characters.demographics: Teenage boy; best friend; age-matched to Alma.
lead_characters.hook: David is Alma’s loyal best friend, but the script gives him real emotional texture: he clings to childhood wonder, protects Alma instinctively, and is quietly terrified of losing the bond that defines his world. He is not just support; he is the person who keeps asking whether belief is worth the risk.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Lucas Hedges in Lady Bird or Fionn Whitehead in The Children Act a chance to be tender without being passive. It offers a young actor a rare best-friend part with emotional agency, comic rhythm, and a pivotal loyalty test.

lead_characters.name: Clerk
lead_characters.demographics: Adult woman; gas station clerk; queer-coded or queer-read presence.
lead_characters.hook: The clerk is a brief but crucial catalyst: she registers Alma’s attraction, mirrors her through visual details, and helps turn the gas station scene into a quiet awakening. She is less a plot function than a charged encounter that Alma cannot fully name yet.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of compact, scene-stealing role that gave Greta Lee in Past Lives or Auliʻi Cravalho in smaller supporting turns a chance to create a whole emotional universe in minutes. It’s a sharp showcase for an actor who can do subtext, warmth, and magnetism with very little screen time.

casting_characteristics: adult supporting woman in a brief but pivotal scene

notable_requirements: simple contemporary suburban or small-town environments

technical.vfx_details: Primarily invisible or light enhancement work for the horn emergence and any subtle magical-realist effects; no large-scale creature or environment build.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood and makeup effects for the horn emergence; sound design is narratively important but not a cost driver on its own.

platform_fit.content_level: PG-13 equivalent with mature thematic material
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; best suited to streaming-first or specialty theatrical with strong festival launch potential.

budget.note: Contemporary, small cast, a handful of practical locations, and only minor VFX for the horn and blood effects keep this comfortably contained.

casting.note: The lead requires a teenage performer who can carry romantic awakening, denial, and body-horror reaction in the same role; the clerk also needs immediate screen presence for a short scene.

development.note: The metaphor is clear, the emotional arc is legible, and the script’s strongest scenes already do the heavy lifting; this is more a packaging and execution conversation than a structural rebuild.

comp_set.title: The Half of It
comp_set.why_it_comps: Shares the queer coming-of-age lane, the intimate emotional scale, and the sense of a young woman discovering herself through a carefully controlled tonal voice.

comp_set.title: The Shape of Water
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on the lyrical fantasy-romance register and the idea of a magical being functioning as a metaphor for desire, difference, and self-acceptance.

comp_set.title: Raw
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the body-horror-as-coming-of-age instinct, where physical transformation becomes the external expression of identity panic and awakening.

comp_set.title: Aftersun
comp_set.why_it_comps: Not genre-matched, but it comps on emotional restraint, memory texture, and the way a small-scale film can land with outsized feeling.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults and older teens who respond to queer coming-of-age stories, elevated fantasy, and emotionally intimate genre films.
audience_target.demographics: Skews female and queer; strongest with 16-34 and 25-44 viewers who watch prestige indie and streamer originals.

budget_tier.note: A small contemporary cast, limited locations, and light practical/VFX work keep this in the specialty indie range.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals teams building prestige genre
specialty distributors seeking festival-friendly breakout titles
indie producers with elevated horror or magical-realist taste
festival-facing buyers looking for awards-adjacent queer material
lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane where emotional authenticity and a distinctive metaphor matter as much as plot mechanics. The script has the kind of controlled, filmable concept that can attract a director with a visual point of view and a buyer looking for a tasteful genre swing.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed emotional arc; the supporting characters are vivid but do not suggest a clean spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The unicorn metaphor is emotionally precise.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the film a clean commercial identity: a fantasy premise that is instantly legible but still feels personal and authorial. Buyers looking for elevated genre can sell the hook in one sentence without flattening the emotional meaning.
strengths.evidence: The recurring shimmer sound, the horn reveal, and the lesbian-flag book stack all build the metaphor without overexplaining it.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The gas station scene is a standout set piece.
strengths.what_it_means: A script with one genuinely memorable scene is much easier to champion in a crowded marketplace, especially when that scene demonstrates tone, subtext, and character all at once. This is the kind of sequence that makes a director and actors want to read the rest.
strengths.evidence: The slushy choice, the clerk encounter, the rude-customer confrontation, and the quiet attraction beat all escalate inside one contained sequence.

strengths.what_it_means: The body-horror turn gives the film a sharper aftertaste than a conventional queer awakening story, which helps it stand out in both festival and streamer conversations. That tonal courage is a real differentiator for buyers hunting for something emotionally accessible but not bland.
strengths.evidence: The horn emerges bleeding and grotesque yet beautiful, making self-discovery feel costly rather than purely triumphant.

strengths.what_it_means: A contained location footprint and limited cast make this easier to package around a director or breakout lead, which lowers the barrier to entry for indie financiers and streamers. It is the kind of concept that can be made well without a giant production footprint.
strengths.evidence: The story plays across a childhood party, a gas station, the woods, and a few simple contemporary spaces.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean elevated-genre buy: a queer coming-of-age feature with a memorable metaphor, one standout set piece, and a contained production footprint. It has the emotional accessibility of prestige indie drama, but the unicorn/body-horror conceit gives buyers a sharper hook than the average identity story.

items.area: The story is built on one central metaphor.
items.detail: The unicorn conceit is strong, but the script’s commercial identity lives almost entirely inside that single idea. That makes the buy highly dependent on whether a producer believes the metaphor lands as emotionally universal rather than niche or overly literary.

items.area: The supporting world is intentionally thin.
items.detail: Outside Alma and David, the script does not build much recurring relationship density or a larger social ecosystem. That keeps the film intimate, but it also limits the number of secondary characters a buyer can point to when thinking about broader audience attachment.

items.area: The lead casting ask is specific.
items.detail: Alma needs a performer who can play wonder, shame, attraction, and physical terror without tipping into performance. That is a meaningful casting filter for a role that has to carry the entire film’s emotional credibility.

items.area: The climax is more emotional than plot-driven.
items.detail: The woods argument and horn reveal are effective, but the script is not building toward a large external payoff or a high-stakes reversal. Buyers will read this as a resonance piece, which is a strength creatively but a narrower commercial lane than a more propulsive genre feature.

issues.headline: The main friction is concentration: the film’s power comes from one metaphor, one central relationship, and one lead performance that has to do a lot of heavy lifting. That makes it elegant and contained, but also more dependent on execution and taste than a broader commercial genre package.
